Scientists have found a new way to suppress the hepatitis B virus using gene editing. Сергей Гармаш • 23.09.2026, 16:31 • Exclusive Discover more Consult Online Doctors Order DNA Kits Track Health Symptoms Read on Telegram Read on Facebook Discover more Order Infection Tests политический Читать Политическую Аналитику Epigenetic treatment methods show promising results in the fight against chronic hepatitis B, a liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), which affects over 250 million people worldwide. Traditional medications often fail to completely eliminate the virus from the body, highlighting the need for new therapeutic approaches. Gene therapy, which is used to make changes to DNA, has been studied before but may increase the risk of cancer in patients with hepatitis B. In response, scientists have begun exploring epigenetic editing—a method that alters markers on DNA, influencing gene activity. Researchers from nChroma Bio, based in Boston, and institutions in Milan, Italy, have developed a way to attach chemical tags to the hepatitis B virus genome, allowing them to suppress its activity and block the production of viral particles. Results from trials on human liver cells and mice showed promising outcomes, with minimal and temporary side effects from the therapy observed in tests on monkeys. These findings were published in the journal Nature Biomedical Engineering on September 21. “The effectiveness of a single injection was quite impressive. This is exactly the direction we need to move in to tackle the hepatitis B virus pandemic,” noted virologist John Tavis from Saint Louis University in Missouri. Angelo Lombardo, a molecular biologist from the San Raffaele Telethon Gene Therapy Institute in Milan, added that the results of preclinical studies confirm the feasibility of applying this approach in clinical practice. nChroma Bio has already begun clinical trials in Hong Kong and New Zealand, with the first participant receiving therapy in January. Lombardo also emphasized that these trials represent a “huge step forward” and are the result of many years of research; however, nChroma Bio declined to comment on the results when approached by Nature. Challenges of Chronic Infection The hepatitis B virus can cause serious health issues as it is capable of hiding in the body and evading the immune response. One such mechanism involves the formation of mini-chromosomes that can persist in liver cells for extended periods. These mini-chromosomes create a “genomic archive of the virus,” which helps it replicate when patients stop taking antiviral medications and contributes to disease relapses, as explained by virologist Fabien Zullim from the University of Lyon in France. Less than 10% of patients undergoing treatment for more than ten years can stop taking medications without the risk of relapse. The virus can also integrate its fragments into the host's DNA and produce proteins that weaken the immune response. The integration of viral DNA causes molecular changes in liver cells, which can lead to cancer. The therapeutic drug CRMA-1001 from nChroma includes a modified Cas9 enzyme from the CRISPR system, which lacks the usual DNA cleavage activity, and also contains RNA strands that guide the enzyme to the target area in the hepatitis B virus genome. Encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles, the therapy suppresses both freely moving and integrated copies of the virus by marking them with methyl groups. In an experiment on mice infected with both types of viral DNA, a single injection of CRMA-1001 significantly reduced the levels of viral DNA and proteins associated with viral activity. In 25 out of 60 animals that received one or three injections, the virus level became undetectable after six months. The safety of three monthly infusions of CRMA-1001 was tested on crab-eating macaques. Although liver enzyme levels increased after administering the maximum dose, they returned to normal within four weeks, and no serious side effects were observed. Future of Treatment nChroma plans to expand its clinical trials to the UK and France, but it is not the only company developing epigenetic treatments for hepatitis B. In May, Tune Therapeutics from Seattle reported preliminary results from its trials testing different doses of its epigenetic inhibitor, demonstrating suppression of viral activity for up to 17 months. Both clinical studies will need to confirm whether these methods can completely eliminate the viral infection and achieve functional cures. Tavis suggests that they could become an important part of comprehensive treatment, but even with a high level of viral suppression, remaining cells may continue to infect the liver. Zullim also emphasizes the need for clinical trials to identify potential side effects of new methods. According to Tavis, it will also be necessary to confirm the absence of risks of off-target epigenetic effects. “These patients will need to be monitored for several years,” he added. doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-02981-9 Read on Telegram Read on Facebook Discover more Compare Prescription Prices Healthcare Book Therapy Sessions Read also: Healthcare The first medical institutions in Kyrgyzstan appeared in the late 19th century: reception rooms in... records.content: India India reaffirms commitment to eliminate Hepatitis B, C as public health threats by 2030 Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava says over 225 million people have been screened and more than 6.52 lakh patients have received free treatment. NEW DELHI: India has reaffirmed its commitment to combating viral Hepatitis and eliminating Hepatitis B and C as public threats by 2030. Addressing a side-event at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA 81), Union Health Secretary, Punya Salila Srivastava, said, “Reaffirming India’s commitment to the 2030 SDG Agenda on combating hepatitis and the global goal of eliminating Hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030.” She highlighted India’s comprehensive, people-centred response across prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and care. “India has strengthened interventions across the continuum - from antenatal screening and Hepatitis B immunisation to free diagnosis and treatment, safe blood transfusion services, and counselling and rehabilitation support for people who inject drugs,” she said at the session “Advancing Global Action to Eliminate Hepatitis” organised by the UN Group of Friends to Eliminate Hepatitis. She further said that the scale of these efforts is reflected in the numbers. More than 225 million beneficiaries have been screened, while over 6,52,000 patients have received free treatment. Srivastava emphasised the importance of sustained global cooperation, equitable access to prevention, testing and treatment, and stronger health systems to accelerate progress towards the 2030 targets. “India remains committed to advancing coordinated, accessible and equitable action to combat viral hepatitis and contribute to its elimination as a public health threat by 2030,” she added. Hepatitis is an inflammation of the liver that is caused by a variety of infectious viruses and non-infectious agents leading to a range of health problems, including severe liver damage and cancer, some of which can be fatal. There are five main strains of the hepatitis virus, referred to as types A, B, C, D and E. According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), types B and C lead to chronic disease in hundreds of millions of people and together are the most common cause of liver cirrhosis, liver cancer and viral hepatitis-related deaths. They are among the main infectious disease killers, causing an estimated 1.3 million deaths per year. Hepatitis has been recognised as a public health problem in India. In 2018, the union government launched the National Viral Hepatitis Program to combat this disease by providing screening and treatment services. This is in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal of combating various viral diseases. According to India's 2021 HIV Sentinel Surveillance data, about 0.85% of people tested positive for Hepatitis B and 0.29% for Hepatitis C - roughly 1 in 118 and 1 in 345 people, respectively. As per WHO, an estimated 304 million people worldwide live with hepatitis B or C, and for most, testing and treatment remain beyond reach. The New Indian Express www.newindianexpress.com

Policy 2 min read India reaffirms commitment to eliminate Hepatitis B, C as public health threats by 2030 Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava highlighted India's comprehensive and people-centred approach towards combating Hepatitis at an event titled "Advancing Global Action to Eliminate Hepatitis", a UNGA 81 side event organised by the UN Group of Friends to Eliminate Hepatitis. ANI Published On Sep 23, 2026 at 12:59 PM IST Select ETHealthworld as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook New Delhi: Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava highlighted India's comprehensive and people-centred approach towards combating Hepatitis at an event titled "Advancing Global Action to Eliminate Hepatitis", a UNGA 81 side event organised by the UN Group of Friends to Eliminate Hepatitis. Addressing the event, Srivastava spoke about India's efforts across prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment and care for Hepatitis. According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, she reaffirmed India's commitment to the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) agenda on combating Hepatitis and the global target of eliminating Hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030. Advt The Union Health Secretary's remarks came as India continues to focus on strengthening measures related to the prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment of Hepatitis, with efforts aimed at addressing the disease burden through a people-centred public health approach. Meanwhile, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has issued an advisory circular to healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers, distributors, hospitals and the general public against the indiscriminate use of painkillers, particularly Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs), and antibiotics, citing associated risks of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), the circular dated September 21 stated that NSAIDs and antibiotics should only be used when clinically indicated, in appropriate doses and for the recommended duration, under the supervision of a Registered Medical Practitioner. The DGHS said that the import, manufacturing, sale and distribution of drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the rules framed thereunder. It further noted that various drugs, including NSAIDs and antibiotics, are placed under Schedules G, H, H1 and X of the Drugs Rules, 1945, depending on their applicability and potential risks, and are required to carry prescribed warnings, cautions and conditions of sale. Advt "Most of the NSAIDs are included in Schedule H of the Drugs Rules, 1945. Thus, they are not to be sold by retail without the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner, as is required in Rule 97 of the Drugs Rules, 1945," the circular stated. Similarly, the DGHS said that most antibiotic drugs are included in Schedule H1 and are required to carry specific warnings. Show original What if you are told you are 'HBsAg positive' in a health checkup? Hepatitis B? A liver specialist explains what to check next 消化器内科医K|胃腸・内視鏡をわかりやすく 2026年9月21日 18:22 When you look at the results of your health checkup or medical examination, “HBsAg positive” was written there. When you search online, “Hepatitis B,” “liver cirrhosis,” “liver cancer” terms like these appear, and some of you may have become anxious. First, what I want you to know is that being HBsAg positive is an important result indicating that you are infected with the hepatitis B virus (HBV). On the other hand, HBsAg positive does not mean that immediate treatment is necessary. It does not mean that. Next, “how much virus is present,” “is there inflammation in the liver,” “to what extent is the liver damaged” we will check these. This time, from the perspective of a liver specialist, I will explain in order what is actually checked after being told you are HBsAg positive in a health checkup. What is “HBsAg” in the first place? HBV stands for Hepatitis B Virus. HBsAg is an indicator derived from a protein on the surface of HBV. If HBsAg is detected in the blood, it basically indicates a state of current HBV infection. The Japan Society of Hepatology also explains that HBV infects the liver and causes hepatitis, and if the infection persists, it may progress from chronic hepatitis to liver cirrhosis and further to hepatocellular carcinoma. However, there is one important thing here. People infected with HBV are not all in the same condition. Some have high viral loads. Some have almost no viral replication. Some have active hepatitis. Some have stable liver function. Some already have advanced liver fibrosis. Their conditions are quite different. Therefore, you cannot determine the future course of action based solely on the HBsAg result. The meaning is completely different from 'HBsAb positive' What is particularly easy to confuse in health checkup results are HBsAg and HBsAb . The names differ by only one character, but their meanings are vastly different. HBsAg positivity is an important finding indicating a current HBV infection. On the other hand, HBsAb becomes positive after a past infection or after receiving the hepatitis B vaccine. In fact, the Japan Society of Hepatology also explains that HBsAb can be acquired through the hepatitis B vaccine. In other words, being 'HBsAb positive' does not mean you are infected with hepatitis B. When looking at your results sheet, first check whether it is an 'antigen' or an 'antibody'. If you are HBsAg positive, the next step is to check for 'HBV-DNA'. When you are HBsAg positive, what is extremely important is HBV-DNA . Simply put, it is a test to see how much hepatitis B virus is in your blood. With HBsAg alone, even if you know you are 'infected', you cannot tell 'how much the virus is currently multiplying'. Therefore, we measure HBV-DNA. The HBV-DNA level is also important information when determining whether treatment is necessary. Even in the latest guidelines from the Japan Society of Hepatology, treatment strategies are determined by combining factors such as HBV-DNA, ALT, and the state of liver fibrosis. Is it okay to leave it alone if ALT is normal? This is a common misunderstanding. For example, AST 24 ALT 20 γ-GTP 25 and only HBsAg was positive. "Since all liver function tests are normal, there's no problem, right?" You might think so. However, normal ALT does not necessarily mean that nothing needs to be done regarding HBV . In HBV infection, it is necessary to consider the state of the virus, liver inflammation, and fibrosis separately. Therefore, HBV-DNA. HBeAg/HBeAb. AST/ALT. Platelet count. Abdominal ultrasound, etc., as needed. are evaluated in combination. I previously explained in detail here what to do if your ALT levels were high during a health checkup. https://note.com/hip_lily5822/n/nafbc45e53bfe ALT is a very important number, but the point that you should not judge the entire liver based on ALT alone is the same for hepatitis B. What are 'HBeAg' and 'HBeAb'? When you visit a medical institution because you are HBsAg positive, HBeAg HBeAb you may encounter these tests with similarly confusing names. In general, HBeAg is one of the indicators used to consider the proliferation status of HBV. However, HBeAg positive does not necessarily mean severe HBeAg negative does not mean you are safe It is not that simple. Even if HBeAg is negative, there are cases where HBV proliferates and causes hepatitis. That is why nowadays, it is important to check HBV-DNA directly . If you are confused by the many test items, you should ask, 'What is my HBV-DNA level?' and that should be helpful. If you are told you are a 'carrier,' do you never have to do anything for the rest of your life? Previously, Some people have been told, "You are a hepatitis B virus carrier, but your liver function is normal, so let's just monitor it." And they have not visited a doctor for a long time since being told that. It is true that some people have stable liver function and do not immediately require antiviral treatment. However, not receiving treatment and not following up are two different things. With HBV infection, the viral load and the state of hepatitis can change over time. Also, it is necessary to assess the risk of liver fibrosis and liver cancer. "Not taking medication does not mean you don't need to go to the hospital." That is not the case. It is important to clarify your current status: Are you in a state that requires treatment? Are you in a state where regular follow-up is sufficient? In that case, what should be checked and at what intervals? It is important to organize these points at least once. "HBsAg positive" does not mean "cirrhosis" Upon hearing they are HBsAg positive, some people worry, "Is my liver already in very bad shape?" However, HBsAg is a test that indicates HBV infection, not a test that diagnoses cirrhosis itself. To see how much the liver is damaged, Platelets. Albumin. Bilirubin. Abdominal ultrasound. Liver stiffness. Other blood and imaging tests. These are combined. Recently, an index called FIB-4, which can be calculated from age, AST, ALT, and platelets, is also widely used as an entry point for considering liver fibrosis. FIB-4 is explained in detail here. https://note.com/hip_lily5822/n/n353d1dceb24a However, in hepatitis B, the condition is not determined by FIB-4 alone. The idea of "not judging the entire liver based on a single number" is important. Will it spread to family members? Is it necessary to separate dishes? HBV is mainly transmitted through blood and body fluids. The Japan Society of Hepatology explains that in adults, infection can occur through sexual intercourse with an infected partner, and familial transmission has also been reported. On the other hand, Being in the same room. Eating together. Shaking hands. It is not something that is easily transmitted through normal daily life. If you find out you are HBsAg positive, regarding your cohabiting family members or partner, Have they ever been tested for HBV? Do they have HBs antibodies? Is vaccination necessary? You should consult a medical institution about these. The Japan Society of Hepatology also recommends considering the hepatitis B vaccine for family members living with someone infected with HBV. What is the difference between those who 'receive treatment' and those who 'are monitored'? I think this is the point of most concern. Treatment for hepatitis B is not, 'Everyone who is HBsAg positive must take medication.' That is not the case. In the 2026 guidelines of the Japan Society of Hepatology, for chronic hepatitis, mainly, ALT, HBV-DNA, and liver fibrosis, are evaluated, and the indication for antiviral treatment is determined, including the presence or absence of cirrhosis. When treatment is necessary, antiviral drugs called nucleoside/nucleotide analogs are currently used. On the other hand, there are cases where treatment is not started immediately, and the condition is monitored while periodically performing blood tests and imaging tests. Therefore, when you are told you are HBsAg positive, "Do I need to take medication?" You don't have to make that your only initial goal. First, "What stage of HBV infection am I currently in?" is what you need to confirm first. What to check when you visit a doctor with your health checkup results If you are HBsAg positive, please bring your results sheet with you instead of throwing it away. If possible, it is also helpful to have your past health checkup results. What I want to confirm is: Is this the first time your HBsAg has been positive? Was it positive in the past as well? What are your AST and ALT levels? What is your platelet count? Have you ever been told you have hepatitis B in the past? Does anyone in your family have hepatitis B? Have you ever had an HBV-DNA test in the past? Have you ever had an abdominal ultrasound? and so on. And when you visit the doctor, "Will you be checking my HBV-DNA?" Please try asking. This is an important next step to organize your current status based on the single result of being HBsAg positive. The way of thinking is different from being HCV antibody positive In yesterday's article, “HCV antibody positive does not necessarily mean you are currently infected with hepatitis C” is what I wrote about. For hepatitis C, we confirm HCV-RNA after an HCV antibody positive result to determine if the virus is currently present. The article is here. https://note.com/hip_lily5822/n/n59c03fe0c6d8 On the other hand, the HBsAg result this time has a different meaning. Even though they are similar results of being “hepatitis virus positive,” it is important not to think of HBsAg positive and HCV antibody positive in the same way. that is important. Do not stop at “positive,” but investigate what comes next It is natural to feel anxious when it is written that you are HBsAg positive. However, from that one line alone, we cannot tell: How much the virus is currently multiplying. Whether hepatitis is occurring. To what extent the liver is damaged. Whether treatment is necessary. is not yet known. Therefore, please consider HBsAg positive not as the finish line, but as the starting point for evaluation. think of it as that. Check HBV-DNA. Check liver function. Evaluate liver fibrosis. Treat those who need it. Follow up those who do not need treatment at the necessary intervals. Once you have organized things this far, there is no need to be more afraid than necessary just by looking at the word 'positive'. If it was found during a health checkup, now that it has been found, it is the right time to properly check your condition once. *This article is intended to provide general medical information and does not provide individual diagnosis or treatment. Treatment indications and follow-up methods for hepatitis B vary depending on HBV-DNA, ALT, liver fibrosis, age, presence of cirrhosis, comorbidities, etc. If you are pointed out as HBsAg positive, please consult a gastroenterology or hepatology department. Show original Epigenome editing to silence hepatitis B without DNA cleavage | CRMA-1001 moves to human trials 1 とりがら 2026年9月22日 12:06 Development of an investigational epigenetic silencer therapy to transcriptionally inactivate viral DNA in chronic hepatitis B (Development of an investigational epigenetic suppression therapy aimed at transcriptional inactivation of viral DNA in chronic hepatitis B) Journal (Publication Date): Nature Biomedical Engineering (September 21, 2026) DOI: 10.1038/s41551-026-01802-8 Corresponding Author/Affiliation: Yesseinia Anglero-Rodriguez et al. (nChroma Bio). Collaborators include Angelo Lombardo of San Raffaele, Milan, among others. Open access. Key Takeaways We developed CRMA-1001, a drug candidate that silences the hepatitis B virus using methylation tags without cutting its DNA. In mice, a single dose reduced viral markers by over three orders of magnitude, and after three doses, surface antigens and viral DNA became undetectable in up to 90% of subjects after six months. In monkeys, transient liver enzyme elevation was observed only at the highest dose. No unintended methylation of the human genome was detected. This is not a paper about a human cure, but rather preclinical research results for a novel therapeutic candidate aimed at achieving functional cure through limited-duration treatment. Chronic hepatitis B: A condition where the virus persists in the liver cccDNA: Circular viral blueprint remaining in the nucleus intDNA: Viral DNA integrated into the human genome Functional cure: HBsAg and HBV DNA remain undetectable for more than six months after stopping medication Epigenome editing: A method to turn off gene expression without altering the DNA sequence Why this research was conducted Chronic hepatitis B affects approximately 250 million people worldwide. Current nucleoside analogs suppress replication, but surface antigens (HBsAg) are difficult to eliminate, leading to relapse upon discontinuation. This is because two types of latent DNA remain. Circular DNA in the nucleus (cccDNA)... the source of replication DNA integrated into the host genome (intDNA)... the source of HBsAg To achieve a functional cure (HBsAg clearance and undetectable HBV DNA for 6+ months after treatment cessation), both must be silenced. DNA-cutting editing carries risks of oncogenesis. Therefore, we are approaching this using non-cutting epigenome editing. Comparison table with existing nucleoside analog treatments What was investigated and how CRMA-1001 contains the following in lipid nanoparticles: Non-cleaving Cas9 (dCas9) Transcriptional repressor domain KRAB Methyltransferase DNMT3A/3L Guide RNA targeting HBV (lead is HBV-gRNA2, approximately 94% conserved across genotypes A-H) 121 guides were screened in cells, and pharmacology, safety, and specificity were evaluated in HepG2 lines, AAV-HBV mice, transgenic mice, and monkeys. Combination therapy with entecavir is also being considered. Key findings Guides were scattered across the genome, and no single specific site was essential The lead guide maintained antigen suppression after cell proliferation, which correlated with the strength of methylation A single dose in mice reduced viral markers by over 3 log10. With three doses, up to 90% showed undetectable HBsAg and HBV DNA at 6 months The design targets both cccDNA and intDNA for suppression In monkeys, only the highest dose showed transient transaminase elevation Expression and methylation analysis in primary human cells detected no unintended targets Experiments silencing PCSK9 with the same platform showed long-term methylation maintenance in monkeys (evidence of platform durability) Strengths and limitations of this study Strengths: Does not cleave. Targets both latent forms simultaneously. Multiple models used. Off-targets evaluated in human cells. Limitations: Efficacy and safety in humans not yet reported (this paper is preclinical). Mouse HBV models are not identical to human chronic infection. Functional cure definition not yet met in humans. Long-term liver regeneration and immune reconstitution in humans remain unknown. What can and cannot be said from this study What can be said: There is preclinical data that HBV transcription can be suppressed for a long time via methylation. This provided the basis for proceeding to clinical trials as a candidate for finite-duration therapy. What cannot be said: It already cures humans. It is safer than conventional drugs. One shot cures everyone. Cancer risk is zero. Common misconceptions | Q&A Has it already cured humans? → No, it is still in the preclinical stage Cure with a single shot? → Results in mice primarily show three doses Safe because it doesn't cut? → No off-target detection does not equal zero risk Will vaccines and nucleic acid analogs become unnecessary? → This paper cannot say Impressions The reason hepatitis B is so troublesome is that even if medication lowers the viral load, latent copies remain in the liver. Furthermore, there are two types of these copies: cccDNA floating in the nucleus and intDNA integrated into the human genome. The distinction that the former is the main body of replication and the latter is the source of surface antigens was easy to understand. This is also the reason why current drugs suppress replication but struggle to eliminate antigens. With that in mind, the author chose not to cut the DNA. Scissors are powerful, but cutting sequences integrated into the host carries the constant worry of carcinogenesis. Therefore, they removed the Cas9 blade and loaded it with a methyltransferase and a transcriptional repression domain to tag the site as "off." The core of this method is that even if the drug itself (dCas9 or guide RNA) is short-lived within the cell, the tag that was pressed can remain. What left an impression in terms of numbers is that even a single dose in mice reduced viral indicators by more than three orders of magnitude, and with three doses, surface antigens and viral DNA became undetectable in up to 90% of cases after six months. However, this is not a human trial. In monkeys, only the highest dose caused a transient rise in liver enzymes. It is written that no unintended methylation was found in human cells. As a preclinical study, the logic holds, but this is not a "cured" article. While reading, I thought about the weight of the term functional cure. The benchmark is that neither antigens nor viral DNA appear for six months after stopping treatment, but what this paper demonstrated was not that it met that definition in humans, but that it "carried a mechanism capable of targeting that definition into animals." Reading this in conjunction with the news that clinical trials have begun in Hong Kong and New Zealand clarifies its positioning. One more thing. The fact that the guide RNA is about 94% conserved across types A through H is subtle but important. Since hepatitis B is divided into types, a single-point breakthrough sequence would not reach the world. The design of placing the methyl group at a conserved site after selecting from 121 candidates seemed to prioritize "reach" over "sharpness." The limitations are also clear. Mouse HBV is not the same as chronic human infection. Whether the tags remain after the liver regenerates, or whether the immune system will recover by chasing the antigen decline, can only be seen in humans. It cannot be definitively said that it is safe because it does not cut. It is considered that off-targets being "invisible to current detection methods" is different from "never occurring." records.content: Home Article Highlight | 24-Sep-2026 qHBsAg trajectories with Peg-IFNα-2b add-on therapy in nucleos(t)ide analog-experienced HBeAg-positive chronic hepatitis B Xia & He Publishing Inc. Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: Among NA‐experienced, HBeAg‐positive CHB patients with baseline HBsAg <3,000 IU/mL, Peg‐IFNα‐2b add‐on therapy was associated with rapid early qHBsAg decline followed by modest rebound, whereas NAs alone showed minimal change. Although between‐group difference in HBsAg loss did not reach statistical significance, a trend toward higher cumulative HBsAg loss was observed in the add‐on group. LOESS trajectories offer an intuitive way to visualise qHBsAg dynamics in small real‐world cohorts with irregular sampling and few endpoint events. view more Credit: Yongning Xin, Yong Zhou HBsAg loss is the preferred endpoint for functional cure in chronic hepatitis B (CHB), but remains uncommon with finite treatment. Peg‐IFNα‐2b may increase HBsAg decline in selected patients, but small real‐world cohorts have limited HBsAg loss events. Binary endpoints do not capture on‐treatment qHBsAg dynamics, which are measured irregularly. This study characterised qHBsAg trajectories using LOESS in NA‐experienced patients receiving Peg‐IFNα‐2b add‐on therapy versus NAs alone. Methods Design: Real‐world, multicentre, prospective cohort study (2023–2025) in Shandong, China. Participants: NA‐experienced, HBeAg‐positive CHB patients with ≥12 months continuous NA therapy and baseline HBsAg <3,000 IU/mL. Exclusions: HCV/HDV/HIV coinfection, other chronic liver diseases, NASH, HCC, telbivudine use. Cohorts: 161 received Peg‐IFNα‐2b add‐on; 205 continued NAs alone. One‐to‐one propensity score matching (PSM) used age, sex, WBC, neutrophils, haemoglobin, platelets, and qHBsAg. Analysis: Piecewise LOESS (span = 0.50) fitted before/after baseline. Kaplan‐Meier estimated cumulative HBsAg loss (≤0.05 IU/mL) with censoring at day 500. Results After PSM, 161 matched pairs were formed with balanced covariates. Median Peg‐IFNα‐2b duration was 315 days (IQR 172–350); 64/161 (39.8%) received ≥48 weeks. qHBsAg trajectories: Peg‐IFNα‐2b add‐on showed rapid decline after initiation, reaching nadir at ~10–12 months (2.48 log10 IU/mL; 95% CI 2.38–2.61), followed by modest rebound. NAs‐alone showed minimal change. By month 10, 81/161 (50.3%) had discontinued Peg‐IFNα‐2b, coinciding with the rebound. HBsAg loss: Within 500 days, 3 patients in the add‐on group achieved HBsAg ≤0.05 IU/mL versus none in NAs‐alone. Kaplan‐Meier showed a trend toward higher cumulative HBsAg loss (log‐rank P = 0.06). Exploratory: WBC and PLT declined early after Peg‐IFNα‐2b then recovered. qHBeAg declined more rapidly in the add‐on group during the first six months. Discussion Peg‐IFNα‐2b add‐on was associated with early qHBsAg decline followed by modest rebound, whereas NAs alone showed minimal change. The rebound may reflect attenuation of interferon‐induced transcriptional repression, allowing partial restoration of cccDNA‐driven transcription. Mechanistically, Peg‐IFNα represses HBV cccDNA via HDAC3‐associated histone modifications and enhances NK‐cell‐mediated inhibition of regulatory T cells. Limitations: Observational study with non‐randomised control; residual confounding possible. Baseline ALT, prior NA duration, adherence, and HBV genotype were incompletely recorded. Selected population limits generalisability. Variable treatment duration may influence trajectory shape. Conclusions Among NA‐experienced, HBeAg‐positive CHB patients with baseline HBsAg <3,000 IU/mL, Peg‐IFNα‐2b add‐on therapy was associated with rapid early qHBsAg decline followed by modest rebound, whereas NAs alone showed minimal change. Although between‐group difference in HBsAg loss did not reach statistical significance, a trend toward higher cumulative HBsAg loss was observed in the add‐on group. LOESS trajectories offer an intuitive way to visualise qHBsAg dynamics in small real‐world cohorts with irregular sampling and few endpoint events. records.content: Home Article Highlight | 20-Sep-2026 Chronic hepatitis b in the Asia-pacific region: Results of the 2023 global burden of disease study Xia & He Publishing Inc. Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: The Asia-Pacific region continues to contribute the largest share of the global CHB burden and now faces persistent gaps despite progress. Although substantial progress has been made in reducing prevalence through immunization, the region is currently off track to meet the WHO 2030 targets for both incidence and mortality. view more Credit: Xinyu Zhao, Hong You Background and Aims The Asia-Pacific region accounts for a larger share of the hepatitis B burden than any other regions of the world, presenting a challenge to meeting the World Health Organization (WHO) 2030 elimination targets. In this study, we aimed to quantify the burden of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) and project its trends through 2030 using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 framework, thereby identifying gaps and priorities for the Asia-Pacific region to achieve WHO 2030 targets. Methods Using data from the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023, we analyzed CHB prevalence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life years. We evaluated temporal trends (1990–2023) using average annual percent changes and projected the 2024–2030 burden using Bayesian age-period-cohort models. Results In 2023, the Asia-Pacific region accounted for 63% of global CHB cases (178.0 million), 66% of deaths (259.1 thousand), and 65% of disability-adjusted life years (8.4 million). Regional prevalence and mortality rates exceeded global averages, although childhood (<5 years) prevalence was comparatively lower (590.3 vs. 1,325.3 per 100,000). East Asia bore the highest absolute burden (99.2 million cases), and South Asia had the largest pediatric caseload. Between 1990 and 2023, Western Asia showed the steepest decline in adult prevalence (−1.99%), whereas Southeast and Central Asia exhibited upward mortality trends. Projections indicate that the Asia-Pacific region is off track to meet the WHO 2030 disease elimination targets, as the prevalence rate in children under five years remains above the 0.1% target threshold and absolute mortality is projected to increase. Conclusions The Asia-Pacific region continues to contribute the largest share of the global CHB burden and now faces persistent gaps despite progress. Although substantial progress has been made in reducing prevalence through immunization, the region is currently off track to meet the WHO 2030 targets for both incidence and mortality. records.content: Home News Obituary Recipes Charity Special ಕನ್ನಡ Live TV RADIO Advertise Contact Us Matrimonial Properties Jobs General Ads Red Chillies Music Ask Dr Greetings Astrology Tribute Of Love Latest Weight-loss drug combination linked to lower uric acid stone volume Thu, Sep 24 Cancer alliance urges more young people in Sussex, Surrey to take HPV vaccine Thu, Sep 24 Early Alzheimer’s detection crucial as new treatment becomes available in India Thu, Sep 24 Menstrual health apps aid awareness, but fertility predictions remain estimates Thu, Sep 24 IL-17 inhibitors linked to higher candidiasis risk in psoriasis study Wed, Sep 23 Diabetes linked to differences in kidney function, electrolyte levels: Study Wed, Sep 23 CDSCO warns against indiscriminate use of painkillers, antibiotics Wed, Sep 23 Health Maternal hepatitis B does not reduce IVF success, study finds Thu, Sep 24 2026 05:46:07 PM By Daijiworld Media Network Daijiworld Media Network - New Delhi New Delhi, Sep 24: Maternal hepatitis B virus infection does not appear to reduce the chances of pregnancy or live birth following in vitro fertilisation (IVF) or intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI), according to a new study. However, researchers found a higher rate of preterm birth among women with hepatitis B. The researchers retrospectively analysed 3,455 first-time fresh IVF or ICSI embryo-transfer cycles carried out at a reproductive medicine centre in China between 2018 and 2020. The study included 811 cycles involving women with maternal hepatitis B virus infection and 2,644 cycles in which neither partner tested positive for hepatitis B surface antigen. After propensity-score matching to account for differences in baseline characteristics, researchers analysed 810 closely matched pairs. The analysis examined outcomes throughout the reproductive process, including oocyte maturation, fertilisation, embryo development, implantation, pregnancy, delivery and neonatal health. After matching, maternal hepatitis B infection was not associated with significant differences in oocyte maturation, normal fertilisation, development of high-quality embryos or blastocyst formation. Clinical pregnancy rates were also comparable between the two groups, at 44.44 per cent among women with hepatitis B and 45.43 per cent among those in the control group. Similarly, the live-birth rate was 32.59 per cent in the hepatitis B group and 32.96 per cent in the control group. Researchers found no significant differences in implantation, miscarriage, stillbirth or ectopic pregnancy rates. Pregnancy-related outcomes, including gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, premature rupture of membranes and caesarean delivery, were also comparable between the groups. However, preterm birth was significantly more common among women with hepatitis B. After matching, 15.73 per cent of births in the hepatitis B group were preterm, compared with 7.78 per cent in the control group. The researchers said the reason for this association remains uncertain. Chronic inflammation, changes in the immune system and effects on placental development could potentially contribute to the increased risk. However, the study did not have detailed information on factors such as viral load, antiviral treatment and liver function. The retrospective, single-centre nature of the study also means that the findings cannot establish that hepatitis B directly causes preterm birth. The researchers said the findings provide reassurance that maternal hepatitis B infection may not substantially reduce the likelihood of successful IVF or ICSI treatment. At the same time, the higher rate of preterm birth highlights the need for further prospective research and may support closer obstetric monitoring of pregnancies affected by hepatitis B. records.content_title: To eliminate hepatitis B by 2030, we must consider a people-centred approach
records.content: Manila Bulletin Lifestyle Health and Wellness To eliminate hepatitis B by 2030, we must consider a people-centred approach Lifestyle | Health and Wellness To eliminate hepatitis B by 2030, we must consider a people-centred approach By MBrand For gastroenterologist, Dr. Janus Ong (center), reaching the goal of elimination requires the hepatitis strategy to shift toward a decentralized, people-centered primary healthcare model. (Photo: Dr. Janus Ong) At the State of the Nation Address (SONA) in July 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. outlined bold commitments to advance Universal Health Care (UHC) in the Philippines . From expanding preventive health benefit packages to broadening financial access to essential outpatient medicines, the administration signaled a renewed resolve to build a healthier nation. Among the most critical battlegrounds in this UHC roadmap is tackling a silent yet deadly public health threat: hepatitis B. The gravity of this challenge cannot be overstated. The World Health Organization’s (WHO) Global Hepatitis Report 2026 delivers a sobering reality: The Philippines remains among the top 10 nations responsible for nearly 70 percent of all global HBV-related deaths . As a clinician on the frontline, I see the tragic consequences of this statistic daily. Chronic hepatitis B is a “silent killer.” For years, it damages the liver without any noticeable symptoms. By the time a patient presents with symptoms of jaundice, persistent fatigue, or abdominal swelling , the infection has often progressed to liver cirrhosis or fatal liver cancer. While recent policy developments point us in the right direction, a fundamental question remains: Are the government’s new strategies enough to achieve the WHO target of eliminating viral hepatitis by 2030? Financial coverage and policy targets are crucial foundations, but money alone will not cure a disease if the healthcare system remains out of reach for the people who need it most. To bridge this gap, we must fundamentally shift our strategy toward a decentralized, people-centered primary healthcare model. Unlocking a people-centered approach through primary care For millions of Filipinos living in rural areas, accessing care requires financial and time investment in traveling long hours to metropolitan specialty hospitals. (Photo: Tarlac Provincial Health Office) Starting in 2027, the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) plans to gradually include diagnostic blood testing panels and targeted therapies under its benefit packages to enable early detection of conditions affecting the kidney, liver, thyroid, and hepatitis B. Complemented by the broadened accreditation of clinics under the Yaman ng Kalusugan Program (YAKAP), these measures promise improved access to screening and consultation. Furthermore, the expansion of the Guaranteed and Accessible Medications for Outpatient Treatment (GAMOT) Program allows eligible PhilHealth members to receive up to ₱20,000 worth of essential outpatient medicines across more than 2,000 accredited providers. Together with the planned expansion of YAKAP benefits for hepatitis B, this financial relief can be life-changing for people living with chronic hepatitis B requiring long-term care. However, continuous care management requires more than financial subsidies. For millions of Filipinos living in rural areas, accessing care currently means taking unpaid leave, spending limited savings on transportation, and traveling long hours to metropolitan specialty hospitals. If we are to achieve true accessibility, we must decentralize services by moving from specialist to primary care settings. Integrating hepatitis screening and routine management into the national primary health protection system—making routine testing as common as checking blood pressure or blood glucose at local health centers—will help to strip away systemic friction, normalize screening, and detect infections early. Proven strategies: Primary care delivers scalable results The StITCH project leverages a people-centred care model for people living with hepatitis in primary healthcare facilities in the Philippines and Vietnam. (Photo: Tarlac Provincial Health Office) Skeptics may question whether primary care health centers and health workers can effectively manage a complex disease historically reserved for specialists. However, real-world evidence demonstrates that they not only can but do so with remarkable success. A landmark proof-of-concept is the Strengthening Integrated Treatment and Care for Hepatitis (StITCH Project), a collaborative initiative involving Gilead Sciences, Harvard Medical School, and the University of the Philippines Manila. Implemented across primary healthcare facilities in the Philippines and Vietnam, StITCH demonstrated the power of empowering trained primary care teams to manage hepatitis B care locally. The results in the Philippines were compelling: Over 31,000 individuals were screened for hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection and 72 percent of those who tested positive returned for follow-up care, while 95 percent of patients eligible for treatment initiated it immediately. This people-centred, one-stop primary care approach streamlined the patient journey from blood screening to consultation, shortening the time to linkage to care from more than four months to less than one week. The takeaway for health administrators and policymakers is undeniable: primary care-led management is not merely an alternative approach. Rather, it is the solution to screening and keeping those diagnosed with hepatitis B linked to long-term care. Dismantling stigma: The final barrier to elimination Imee (right), an ambassador for Gilead’s BehinD the SilenCe campaign, believes that her lived experience with hepatitis B gives her purpose to speak for the community to reduce stigma and get the support they need. (Photo: Gilead Sciences) Even the best-funded, most decentralized health infrastructure will fall short if societal fear prevents those diagnosed with hepatitis B from walking through the clinic doors. Heavy social stigma, discrimination, and widespread misinformation continue to keep millions of Filipinos in the shadows, reluctant to seek testing, care, or disclose their status. Overcoming this requires elevating the voices of those with lived experience. Volunteer leaders like Imee, a hepatitis B ambassador with the Yellow Warriors Society Philippines (YWSP), demonstrate the transformative impact of patient advocacy. After resigning from her job out of fear that her colleagues would learn about her hepatitis B diagnosis, Imee understands firsthand how crippling stigma can be. She has transformed that adversity into action, working tirelessly to demystify the disease and challenge cultural taboos. In addition to providing psychological counseling to empower those living with hepatitis, Imee’s work at YWSP also includes mapping local public health services to encourage more people to get screened and access continuous care. Through public awareness initiatives like Gilead Sciences’ BehinD the SilenCe campaign, developed in collaboration with the World Hepatitis Alliance, advocates are shining a light on the unspoken emotional and social burdens of living with hepatitis. By fostering open, empathetic dialogue, we can replace fear with understanding, encouraging individuals to step forward for screening and care without shame. The road ahead: A call for action Viral hepatitis is a preventable and manageable condition. We possess effective strategies and intervention mechanisms on how to screen and deliver care efficiently. However, the roadmap to eliminating viral hepatitis by 2030 requires a unified, multi-sectoral strategy focused on three imperatives: 1. Decentralize services : Fully integrate HBV screening and care into primary care settings, ensuring seamless procurement and distribution of diagnostics and medicines to local health centers.. 2. Capacity building : Train and equip primary care healthcare workers to screen, diagnose, counsel, and manage patients living with hepatitis B in community settings. 3. Community-led advocacy : Partner with patient organizations to normalize public discussions, combat stigma, and overcome barriers to testing and care We stand at a pivotal crossroads. By moving hepatitis care out of specialized hospitals and into primary care community settings, we can transform national policy into saved lives. The time to act is now. records.content: Thursday, September 24, 2026 Login Register Campaign Agency Entertainment Innovation Marketing Creators No Result View All Result Campaign Agency Entertainment Innovation Marketing Creators No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Burnet Institute & Hepatitis B Voices Australia Bust Hepatitis B Myths with “You Can’t Get Hep B Here” Campaign by Indie Creative & Media Agency Enigma by Roastbrief September 22, 2026 in Agency, Entertainment Reading Time: 4 mins read A A A A Reset Share on FacebookShare on Twitter For Australia’s Chinese and Vietnamese communities, misinformation about hepatitis B can cause stigma and shame for people living with the virus. Though the virus is transmitted only through contact with infected blood and sexual fluids, for generations there have been misconceptions that it can be spread through casual contact – simple everyday things like holding hands, hugging or sharing food and utensils. Consequently, people living with hepatitis B have experienced unwarranted social prejudice as friends and even family avoid physical contact and exclude them from social gatherings and the simple everyday pleasure of sharing a meal together. As a result, although hepatitis B treatment is readily available, safe and highly effective, many people avoid diagnosis and care, and, in Australia, three people die from hepatitis B every day. To dispel the damaging myths at the heart of this problem, Burnet Institute – one of Australia’s leading independent medical research and public health institutes – and Hepatitis B Voices Australia (a community-first-led organisation governed by people living with and affected by the virus) have partnered with indie Creative & Media agency Enigma to launch a national campaign with a singular powerful message: “You Can’t Get Hep B Here”. The campaign was co-designed with community members to ensure the messaging is culturally relevant and grounded in the lived experience of people with hepatitis B. The cornerstone of the creative is an adhesive red tape, designed and created by the agency, bearing the campaign’s message in simplified Chinese, Vietnamese and English. The tape, purposely made to make people stop, pause and reassess, was community tested for cultural impact and relevance, with the colour red holding different meanings for different audiences – from warning to hope or celebration. Aldo Ferretto, Enigma Head of Art & Creative Director said, “Our design borrows from the conventional visual language of hazard warning, then deliberately turns it on its head, effectively ‘warning’ our audience that there’s nothing to worry about. The message is beautifully simply clear: the myths aren’t true; you can’t get Hep B here.” The Enigma team meticulously hand-wrapped a suite of familiar everyday objects with the tape. Photographer Andy Lewis photographed the wrapped objects in studio – providing the visual assets that roll out across the campaign’s website and OOH and digital media executions. An installation at Chatswood Mall featured a fully tape-wrapped dining table and chairs set up ready for a meal, inviting the public to sit down and engage with its message. “This idea is all the more powerful when it enters the physical world,” Ferretto said. “Making things with our hands is part of our creative culture at Enigma, and the public’s response to this work is testament to the value of crafting bespoke tangible experiences of this kind.” Associate Professor Jessica Howell, Senior Research Fellow and Head, Hepatitis B and Liver Cancer at the Burnet Institute, said the campaign responds to a critical gap in community knowledge. “For more than 50 years, the Burnet Institute has been working to understand, prevent and ultimately eliminate hepatitis B. We know that fear is one of the biggest obstacles, and when hepatitis B feels threatening or embarrassing, people avoid information altogether.” Hepatitis B Voices Australia, the only community-first-led organisation in Australia completely governed by people living with and affected by hepatitis B, ensures that the people most affected by the condition are central to the national response. Lien Tran, a spokesperson for HBVA, said the community’s involvement in shaping this campaign made a real difference. “For a long time, misinformation has caused so much unnecessary shame and isolation for people living with hepatitis B. This campaign speaks the truth in our languages, in our voices, and it reflects what our communities need to hear,” Ms Tran said. Find out more at www.livewellwithhepb.com.au Credits: Project Partner: Burnet Institute Emily, Adamson, Health Promotion Lead Dr Jack Wallace, Senior Researcher Dr Jacqui Richmond, Program Manager, Workforce & Development Filip Djordjevic, Evaluation Officer Project Partner : Hepatitis B Voices Australia Lien Tran, Project Co-ordinator & Director Dr Thomas Tu, Director Zhenni Jiang, Chinese Peer Navigator Ha Nguyen, Vietnamese Peer Navigator Australian Centre for Disease Control supported the campaign. It is transmitted through contact with infectious blood or body fluids, including sexual contact, sharing needles, birth to an infected mother, and exposure to contaminated blood. Infection can range from asymptomatic to severe liver disease. Symptoms of acute infection include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark urine, joint pain, and jaundice. Many people show no symptoms for years. Risk factors include living in regions where HBV is prevalent, high-risk behaviors, healthcare work involving blood exposure, and multiple sexual partners. Diagnosis involves blood tests that detect HBV antigens and antibodies to determine whether the virus is present, whether the infection is acute or chronic, and the extent of liver damage. Liver function tests and imaging may also be used. Acute Hepatitis B may not require specific treatment, as the body can clear the virus on its own in many cases. Chronic infection is treated with antivirals to suppress viral replication and protect the liver. records.content: Hepatitis B is a disease in which the hepatitis B virus, HBV, causes inflammation of the liver. If it becomes chronic, it can lead to cirrhosis or liver cancer, so patients should, when necessary, manage the condition by taking antiviral medication consistently. In particular, stopping antiviral medication on oneâs own during treatment can allow the virus to replicate again and worsen hepatitis, so caution is required. In severe cases, it can progress to liver failure with a rapid decline in liver function. Health Chosun summarized a case from the Korea Medical Dispute Mediation and Arbitration Agencyâs mediation records in which a patient being treated for hepatitis B stopped antiviral medication and took herbal medicine, after which her liver function deteriorated and she died. âCase overview A, a woman in her 50s, had been taking antiviral medication for chronic hepatitis B since around 2009. From May 2019 she took the antiviral drug Viread tablets, and in August of the same year she received an in-person consultation at B Korean Medicine Clinic and was prescribed Saenggan-tang. For about four months thereafter, she received additional prescriptions for Saenggan-tang via telephone consultations. In November 2019 A stopped taking Viread. Afterwards her liver enzyme levels rose and she experienced indigestion, nausea, and fatigue. In December of that year, the indicators used to assess liver cell damage, AST, GOT, rose to 240 IU/L and ALT, GPT, rose to 495 IU/L. During a January 2020 telephone consultation, medical staff at B Korean Medicine Clinic, having noted this condition, advised A to seek hospital care and to be admitted to a higher-level hospital. However, about five days later Aâs ALT rose to 1000 IU/L and jaundice appeared, and she was admitted to another hospital. Despite receiving antiviral treatment, about a week later she developed hepatic encephalopathy with decreased consciousness. She was transferred to another hospital to consider the possibility of a liver transplant, but liver function did not recover, and after continued treatment at several hospitals she ultimately died. âFamily, âDue to herbal medicine and stopping medicationâ vs Clinic, âNo evidence Saenggan-tang caused side effectsâ The family argued that the herbal medicineâs toxicity and the discontinuation of antiviral medication contributed to Aâs rapid deterioration. They also said that although A complained of abnormal symptoms, appropriate measures were not taken and the opportunity for timely treatment was missed. By contrast, B Korean Medicine Clinic denied there was any basis to conclude that Saenggan-tang caused Aâs rapid deterioration and death. â"Causality not confirmedâ¦ explanations and monitoring were insufficient" The Mediation Agency judged that it was difficult to view the mere prescription of Saenggan-tang to A as inappropriate, and that a clear causal relationship between Saenggan-tang and acute-on-chronic liver failure was not established. Because B Korean Medicine Clinic knew that A planned to stop the antiviral medication she had been taking for a long time, the agency said the clinic should have sufficiently explained the possibility of viral reactivation and hepatitis worsening after stopping the medication, the need for ongoing testing, and similar risks. It also found that although A reported indigestion, nausea, and fatigue and her liver enzyme levels rose significantly after stopping the antiviral medication, the clinicâs follow-up observation was inadequate, for example by not recommending an in-person examination or additional testing. However, the agency found insufficient evidence that B Korean Medicine Clinic directly encouraged the discontinuation of the antiviral medication, and it was also difficult to conclude that the inadequate explanations and follow-up observation directly caused Aâs liver failure and death. The agency noted that A herself did not immediately accept the recommendation for hospitalization, which also contributed to the missed opportunity for appropriate treatment. In the end, the Mediation Agency concluded that B Korean Medicine Clinic did not adequately fulfill its duty to explain and to monitor progress, thereby infringing on Aâs right to choose treatment and opportunity for early treatment, and proposed a settlement awarding the bereaved family 20 million won in compensation. Both parties accepted this proposal and the mediation was concluded. âDo not stop hepatitis B medication on your ownâ¦ be cautious with herbal medicine and supplements Patients with chronic hepatitis B should not stop antiviral medication on their own. Antiviral drugs suppress viral replication to reduce liver damage, and stopping them can allow the virus to increase again and worsen hepatitis. Decisions about stopping medication should be made with medical staff based on liver condition, viral load, and treatment response, and after stopping medication the virus and liver enzyme levels should be regularly monitored. When taking herbal medicine or dietary supplements, it is also advisable to inform medical staff that you have liver disease and to tell them what medications you are currently taking. Not all herbal medicines or supplements are harmful to the liver, but some ingredients can cause liver damage, and products that combine multiple ingredients can make it difficult to identify the cause if problems arise. Latest Current Affairs - 2026-2027 Discover more Health South Asians & Diaspora Vaccines & Immunizations India has set a target to eliminate Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C as public health threats by 2030. The commitment is linked to the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme (NVHCP), which was launched in 2018 and aligns with Sustainable Development Goal 3.3 on ending major communicable diseases. National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme The NVHCP is a national public health programme for prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, and awareness related to viral hepatitis. It provides free services for Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C through district hospitals and other public health facilities. The NVHCP was launched in 2018 as a people-centred health strategy. The programme covers screening, diagnosis, treatment, and referral services. The programme uses public health facilities to expand access to hepatitis care. Hepatitis B and C in Public Health Hepatitis B and Hepatitis C are viral infections that affect the liver and can lead to chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Hepatitis B can spread from mother to child during childbirth, through infected blood, and through unsafe injections or unprotected sexual contact. Hepatitis C mainly spreads through infected blood and unsafe medical procedures. Hepatitis B has a vaccine, while Hepatitis C does not have a vaccine and is treated with antiviral medicines. Screening, Vaccination, and Treatment Measures India follows universal screening of pregnant women for Hepatitis B. Newborns receive a Hepatitis B birth dose within 24 hours of birth under the Universal Immunisation Programme, followed by additional doses at 6, 10, and 14 weeks. The programme also uses affordable generic medicines for Hepatitis B and C treatment. As of 28 July 2026, the NVHCP had screened over 21 crore beneficiaries and provided treatment to about 6.12 lakh patients across 1,153 treatment sites. Discover more Educational Resources Science Technology MCQs India Current Affairs Important Facts for Exams World Hepatitis Day is observed on 28 July every year. Hepatitis B vaccine is included in India’s Universal Immunisation Programme. Hepatitis C has no vaccine, but it is curable with antiviral treatment. Sustainable Development Goal 3.3 covers the fight against communicable diseases by 2030. Integration with Other Health Programmes India’s hepatitis response is linked with the Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child, Adolescent Health and Nutrition programme, the National AIDS Control Programme, the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme, and Blood Transfusion Services. These linkages support screening and referral across multiple public health platforms. Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava reaffirmed the 2030 elimination target at a United Nations General Assembly side event in New York on 23 September 2026. Union Minister of State for Health and Family Welfare Anupriya Patel urged states and Union Territories to intensify awareness on transmission, testing, and treatment in July 2026. Each 10 dB/m CAP increase was associated with a 14% lower risk of liver-related events. Longitudinal CAP monitoring added prognostic value beyond liver stiffness measurements alone. CONTROLLED attenuation parameter dynamics independently predicted liver-related events in patients with chronic hepatitis B receiving antiviral therapy, suggesting that longitudinal monitoring may provide additional prognostic information. The association persisted after accounting for changes in liver stiffness measurements. The study included 573 patients with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who had significant fibrosis or cirrhosis before starting antiviral therapy. Hepatic steatosis was assessed using the controlled attenuation parameter (CAP), while liver-related events included hepatic decompensation, hepatocellular carcinoma, liver transplantation, or liver-related death. Patients were followed for a median of 6.9 years, during which 51 liver-related events occurred. Joint models were used to examine associations between longitudinal measurements and subsequent event risk. Higher CAP Associated With Reduced Risk Dynamic changes in CAP independently predicted liver-related events. Each 10 dB/m increase in CAP was associated with a lower risk of these outcomes (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]: 0.86; 95% CI: 0.78–0.96; p=0.006). The association remained after adjustment for liver stiffness measurement (LSM) dynamics (aHR per 10 dB/m CAP increase: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.77–0.95; p=0.005). CAP measurements exceeding 236 dB/m over time were also associated with a reduced risk of liver-related events (aHR: 0.67; 95% CI: 0.53–0.84; p<0.001). CAP Monitoring Adds Prognostic Information Combining longitudinal CAP and LSM measurements improved prediction compared with LSM dynamics alone. The 7-year area under the receiver operating characteristic curve increased from 0.70 with LSM alone to 0.75 when CAP and LSM dynamics were integrated. The findings demonstrate an association between longitudinal CAP changes and liver-related event risk among patients with CHB and significant fibrosis receiving antiviral therapy. They also indicate that monitoring CAP over time could provide prognostic information beyond liver stiffness dynamics alone. Longitudinal CAP assessment may therefore offer additional value for evaluating liver-related risk during antiviral treatment in this population. Reference Ai X et al. Dynamic changes in controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) improve prognostic prediction for CHB patients with significant fibrosis and cirrhosis. records.content: Latest Upendra Kushwaha calls opposition language inappropriate over electoral roll dispute Anees Bazmee recalls Mushtaq Khan’s iconic line in ‘Welcome’ following his death Varanasi police boost crowd management for October air show Manu Kumar Singh arrested in JSSC-CGL case; two others in remand Govinda praises Anupam Kher as one of India’s finest actors Shambhavi Choudhary urges Bihar CM for women’s safety and justice Friday, 25 September About Contact ADVERTISEMENT Menu Home Opinion Politics Northeast India Arunachal Pradesh Assam Manipur Meghalaya Mizoram Nagaland Sikkim Tripura Nation & Beyond Visual Stories TNM Earth Business Startup TNM Buzz Sports Entertainment Cinema Music Home » Nation and Beyond » India commits to eliminating hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030 Nation and Beyond India commits to eliminating hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030 By TNM (With ANI Inputs) ✓ 23 September 2026, 8:32 am 2 min read 23 Sep 2026 ANI Photo | India commits to eliminating hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030 Union Health Secretary Punya Salila Srivastava emphasised India’s comprehensive, people-centred strategy for combating hepatitis during the event “Advancing Global Action to Eliminate Hepatitis”, a side event of the UN General Assembly’s 81st session organised by the UN Group of Friends to Eliminate Hepatitis. Speaking at the event, Srivastava outlined India’s efforts in prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, and care for hepatitis. She reaffirmed the country’s commitment to the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals agenda aimed at combating hepatitis and meeting the global target of eliminating hepatitis B and C as public health threats by 2030. ADVERTISEMENT Stay connected Make The News Mill your preferred source See more TNM stories when you search for news on Google. Add TNM on Google This commitment comes as India continues to enhance measures for prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment of hepatitis through a people-centred public health approach to address the disease burden. Separately, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) issued an advisory circular on September 21 cautioning healthcare professionals, pharmacists, retailers, distributors, hospitals, and the public against the indiscriminate use of painkillers, particularly Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs), and antibiotics due to the risk of chronic kidney disease (CKD). ADVERTISEMENT The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) stated that NSAIDs and antibiotics should only be used when clinically indicated, in appropriate doses, and for the recommended duration under the supervision of a Registered Medical Practitioner. The DGHS noted that the import, manufacture, sale, and distribution of drugs are regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and its rules, including the Drugs Rules, 1945. Various drugs such as NSAIDs and antibiotics are classified under Schedules G, H, H1, and X according to their risks and conditions of sale. The circular emphasised that most NSAIDs fall under Schedule H, meaning they cannot be sold by retail without a prescription from a Registered Medical Practitioner in accordance with Rule 97 of the Drugs Rules, 1945. Similarly, most antibiotic drugs are classified under Schedule H1 and must carry specific warnings. Events Mumbrella Pro Podcast Jobs Board About Advertise Subscribe Member Exclusives: Dashboard Become a member Campaigns News Burnet Institute and Enigma tackle hepatitis B stigma with myth-busting campaign Zac Nikolovski September 22, 2026 11:15 Indie agency Enigma has wrapped everyday objects in red tape to challenge long-held myths about hepatitis B transmission The Burnet Institute and Hepatitis B Voices Australia have teamed up with independent agency Enigma to tackle long-held misconceptions about hepatitis B, launching a campaign aimed at reducing stigma in Australia’s Chinese and Vietnamese communities. The campaign dubbed “You Can’t Get Hep B Here” seeks to address harmful social stigmas about those living with the disease. For many people in Australia’s Chinese and Vietnamese communities, hepatitis B remains heavily stigmatised due to persistent myths about how the virus is transmitted. Despite only spreading through infected blood and sexual fluids, misconceptions around casual contact remain widespread. Enjoying Mumbrella? Sign up for our free daily newsletter. As a result, people living with hepatitis B can face discrimination, with friends and family avoiding physical contact or even sharing meals with them. ADVERTISEMENT The campaign’s creative is built around an adhesive red tape adorned with the campaign’s messaging in simplified Chinese, Vietnamese and English that is hand-wrapped around everyday objects which were then photographed by Andy Lewis. Designed to instantly snatch the attention of the community and prompt reflection, the tape was community tested for cultural impact and relevance – the colour red symbolises both hope and celebration. The campaign will roll out across OOH and online, paired with an activation at Chatswood Mall which features a dining table and chairs wrapped entirely in the red tape, bringing the campaign’s messaging into the physical world. Creative Quotes Aldo Ferretto, head of art and creative director at Enigma: “Our design borrows from the conventional visual language of hazard warning, then deliberately turns it on its head, effectively ‘warning’ our audience that there’s nothing to worry about. The message is beautifully simply clear: the myths aren’t true; you can’t get Hep B here. “This idea is all the more powerful when it enters the physical world... Making things with our hands is part of our creative culture at Enigma, and the public’s response to this work is testament to the value of crafting bespoke tangible experiences of this kind.” Jessica Howell, senior research fellow and head, hepatitis B and liver cancer at the Burnet Institute: “For more than 50 years, the Burnet Institute has been working to understand, prevent and ultimately eliminate hepatitis B. We know that fear is one of the biggest obstacles, and when hepatitis B feels threatening or embarrassing, people avoid information altogether.” Lien Tran, spokesperson for Hepatitis B Voices Australia: “For a long time, misinformation has caused so much unnecessary shame and isolation for people living with hepatitis B. This campaign speaks the truth in our languages, in our voices, and it reflects what our communities need to hear.” Campaign credits Project Partner: Burnet Institute Emily, Adamson, Health Promotion Lead Dr Jack Wallace, Senior Researcher Dr Jacqui Richmond, Program Manager, Workforce & Development Filip Djordjevic, Evaluation Officer Project Partner : Hepatitis B Voices Australia Lien Tran, Project Co-ordinator & Director Dr Thomas Tu, Director Zhenni Jiang, Chinese Peer Navigator Ha Nguyen, Vietnamese Peer Navigator Australian Centre for Disease Control supported the campaign. records.content: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Science 23 Sep 2026 11:35 pm AEST Date Time Discover more Police news reports news University news section Xia & He Publishing Inc. The impact of baseline liver fibrosis severity on the effectiveness of pegylated interferon (Peg-IFN) combined with nucleos(t)ide analogs (NAs) in the treatment of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg)-positive chronic hepatitis B (CHB) has not been fully clarified. This study aimed to investigate whether the effectiveness of this combination therapy differed according to the severity of baseline liver fibrosis. Methods A total of 172 HBeAg-positive CHB patients receiving Peg-IFN plus NAs were stratified according to non-invasive fibrosis markers (aspartate aminotransferase-to-platelet ratio index [APRI] and fibrosis-4 index [FIB-4]) into three groups: no significant fibrosis (n = 75), significant fibrosis (n = 70), and advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis (n = 27). The primary outcome was the HBeAg clearance rate at 24 months of treatment. Secondary outcomes included the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) clearance rate, the rate of HBsAg level decline > 1.0 log 10 , virological response, and improvement in non-invasive fibrosis indices. Results At 24 months, HBsAg clearance and complete virological response rates were comparable across the three groups. Cumulative HBeAg clearance rates differed significantly (log-rank P = 0.027): 16.00%, 30.00%, and 40.74% in the three groups, respectively, with Group 3 higher than Groups 1 and 2. Multivariate analysis identified a significantly higher likelihood of HBeAg clearance in Group 3 versus Group 1 (adjusted odds ratio = 6.373, 95% confidence interval: 1.288–31.531, P = 0.023). Additionally, analysis of liver fibrosis outcomes showed that patients with more severe baseline fibrosis had a higher proportion of improvement in non-invasive fibrosis indices, with 95.00% in Group 3, while 42.98% of the overall cohort achieved fibrosis improvement. Discover more Online newspaper access Science news updates Stream History Documentaries Conclusions This study demonstrates that baseline liver fibrosis severity is a key independent factor in predicting treatment response to Peg-IFNα plus NAs in patients with HBeAg-positive CHB. Patients with more advanced fibrosis achieved higher rates of HBeAg clearance and substantial improvements in non-invasive fibrosis indices. The robustness of these primary conclusions was supported by sensitivity analyses. These results suggest that baseline fibrosis assessment has clinical value in optimizing patient selection for Peg-IFN-based combination therapy. Future prospective, multicenter studies with long-term follow-up and incorporation of histological or multi-omics approaches are warranted to validate these findings and elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Preterm birth occurred in 15.73% of the hepatitis B group versus 7.78% of controls. Prospective studies are needed to determine whether hepatitis B directly affects preterm birth. MATERNAL hepatitis B virus infection does not appear to reduce the likelihood of pregnancy or live birth following in vitro fertilisation or intracytoplasmic sperm injection, according to new research. However, the study identified a higher rate of preterm birth among women with hepatitis B. Comparing Assisted-Reproduction Outcomes Researchers retrospectively analysed 3,455 first-time fresh IVF or ICSI embryo-transfer cycles performed at a reproductive medicine centre in China between 2018 and 2020. The cohort included 811 cycles involving women with maternal hepatitis B virus infection and 2,644 cycles in which neither partner had hepatitis B surface antigen. Propensity-score matching was used to account for differences in baseline characteristics, producing 810 closely matched pairs. The analysis considered outcomes across the reproductive pathway, including oocyte maturation, fertilisation, embryo development, implantation, pregnancy, delivery and neonatal health. Pregnancy and Live-Birth Rates Unaffected Following matching, maternal hepatitis B infection was not associated with significant differences in oocyte maturation, normal fertilisation, high-quality embryo development or blastocyst formation. Clinical pregnancy rates were comparable between the hepatitis B and control groups, at 44.44% and 45.43%, respectively. Live-birth rates were also similar, at 32.59% among women with hepatitis B and 32.96% among controls. No significant differences were found in implantation, miscarriage, stillbirth or ectopic-pregnancy rates. Rates of gestational hypertension, gestational diabetes, premature rupture of membranes and caesarean delivery were also comparable. Higher Rate of Preterm Birth Preterm birth was the principal outcome that differed between groups. After matching, 15.73% of births in the hepatitis B group were preterm, compared with 7.78% in the control group. The researchers noted that the reason for this association remains uncertain. Chronic inflammation, immune changes and effects on placental development represent possible explanations, but detailed information on viral load, antiviral treatment and liver function was unavailable. The retrospective, single-centre design also means the findings cannot establish that hepatitis B directly causes preterm birth. Nevertheless, the results offer reassurance that maternal hepatitis B infection may not substantially compromise the probability of IVF or ICSI success. The elevated preterm-birth rate warrants confirmation in prospective studies and may support closer obstetric monitoring of affected pregnancies. Reference Jiang W et al. The impact of maternal hepatitis B virus infection on IVF/ICSI-assisted pregnancy outcomes: a propensity score-matched cohort study. Front Med. 2026;13:1925066.
